`get.optimal.armor.combos()` ranks armor combinations using a single number, `SCORE_RAW`
(and its percentile form, `SCORE_PCT`). This vignette explains where that number comes from.

## The problem: metrics on different scales

An armor combination is described by ten metrics: physical, strike, slash, and thrust defense;
magic, fire, and lightning defense; and bleed, poison, and curse resistance. These aren't on
comparable scales. Combined physical defense across a full set of gear typically runs from the
teens up into the hundreds; combined curse resistance rarely gets past a few dozen. A weight of
"1" on physical defense and "1" on curse resistance would not mean equal importance if the raw
values were just added together - physical defense would dominate the total purely because its
numbers are bigger, not because the `weights` argument said so.

The fix is standardization: express each metric in units of "how unusual is this value", not
its raw number. `get.optimal.armor.combos()` does this using the population mean and standard
deviation of each metric, computed once across every possible armor combination (including
every upgrade level) when the package's data was built - see `create_rda/create_rda.R`. These
live in the package's internal data as `means`, `stddevs`, and `corrs` (the population
correlation matrix across the ten metrics).

## Building a score from weights

Given a `weights` vector (one weight per metric, after the function normalizes it to sum to 1),
the package computes a set of per-metric scalars:

```r
score.scalars <- weights / (stddevs * sqrt((t(weights) %*% corrs %*% weights)[1, 1]))
```

For a combination with combined metric values $x_1, \dots, x_{10}$, the score is:

$$
\text{SCORE} = \sum_{i=1}^{10} \text{score.scalars}_i \cdot (x_i - \mu_i)
$$

where $\mu_i$ is that metric's population mean (`means[i]`). This is a weighted, centered sum -
but the *particular* denominator in `score.scalars` isn't arbitrary. It's chosen so that
`SCORE` always has variance exactly 1, no matter what weights are passed in.

To see why: let $\Sigma$ be the population covariance matrix implied by `stddevs` and `corrs`
(so $\Sigma_{ij} = \sigma_i \sigma_j \cdot \text{corr}_{ij}$), and let
$k = \sqrt{w^\top \text{corr} \, w}$ be the normalizing term inside `score.scalars`. Then
`score.scalars` $= w / (\sigma k)$ element-wise, and the variance of SCORE works out to:

$$
\text{Var}(\text{SCORE}) = \text{score.scalars}^\top \Sigma \, \text{score.scalars}
= \frac{1}{k^2} w^\top \text{corr} \, w = \frac{1}{k^2} \cdot k^2 = 1
$$

This is what makes scores comparable across *different* weight choices: a `SCORE_RAW` of 1.5
means "one and a half standard deviations above average for this combination of priorities",
regardless of which priorities were chosen. `tests/testthat/test-scoring.R` checks this
algebraic identity directly, for a battery of random weight vectors.

## Why each armor slot subtracts a quarter of the mean

The four armor slots (head, chest, hands, legs) are scored independently and then added
together - `optimal_armor_combinations()` sums `curr_head_SCORE + curr_chest_SCORE +
curr_hands_SCORE + curr_legs_SCORE`; see `R/optimal-combos.R`, where each slot's contribution
is computed as `score.scalars[i] * (metric_i - 0.25 * means[i])`.

`means[i]` is the population mean of the *combined* metric across a full four-piece
combination, not any one slot's mean. Subtracting `0.25 * means[i]` in each of the four slots,
and then summing all four, subtracts exactly `means[i]` from the total - which is what actually
needs to happen for the total score to be centered at 0. The even four-way split is simply the
easiest way to divide that single subtraction across four separately-computed slot scores; it
doesn't require (and isn't affected by) whether any individual slot's own average metric value
happens to be exactly a quarter of the combo-level mean.

## From SCORE_RAW to SCORE_PCT

Since `SCORE_RAW` is a sum of many roughly-independent standardized quantities, it's
approximately normally distributed. `SCORE_PCT` applies the standard normal cumulative
distribution function to `SCORE_RAW`:

```r
SCORE_PCT <- pnorm(SCORE_RAW, mean = 0, sd = 1)
```

giving an approximate percentile: 100% is (approximately) the best score achievable for the
weights given, 0% the worst, and 50% is exactly average. This is an approximation - the true
distribution of scores across all possible combinations isn't exactly normal - but it's
generally accurate enough to give an intuitive sense of how good a combination is, without
needing to know the score's scale.

## What this does and doesn't let you compare

Because `Var(SCORE) = 1` holds for any weights, scores are directly comparable across different
filter and constraint choices *as long as the weights are held fixed* - a `SCORE_PCT` of 90%
under one set of filters really is better than 80% under a different set of filters, provided
both used the same `weights`. Scores computed with *different* weights are not directly
comparable to each other in the same way, since each weight vector defines its own notion of
"average" combination.
